speaker: John Schulman
title: John Schulman (OpenAI Cofounder) — Reasoning, RLHF, & plan for 2027 AGI
question: In RLHF post-training, why do language models end up persistently more verbose than many users actually want?
guest: There might be some biases in the labeling that lead to verbosity, like the fact that we tend to train for one message at a time rather than the full interaction. If you only see one message, then something that just has a clarifying question or a short response with an invitation to follow up is going to look less complete than something that covers all possibilities. There's also a question of whether people's preferences change depending on how fast the model is streaming its output. Clearly, if you're sitting there waiting for the tokens to come out, you're going to prefer that it gets to the point. But if it just gives you a dump of text instantly, maybe you don't actually care if there's a bunch of boilerplate—if there's a bunch of stuff you're going to skim, you'd rather just have it all there.

points.core: Preference labeling typically optimizes isolated single messages instead of full conversations.
points.note: Accept: single-turn rating setup, evaluating one turn at a time rather than multi-turn dialogue outcomes. Do not credit: generic claims that raters blindly pick longer text without explaining the single-message evaluation unit.

points.core: Short clarifying questions appear less complete than exhaustive single-turn answers.
points.note: Accept: brief responses, follow-up invitations, or clarifying questions losing to comprehensive replies that cover every possibility in one shot. Do not credit: vague mentions of length bias without contrasting concise or clarifying replies against exhaustive coverage.

points.core: Slow token streaming makes users prefer concise, direct responses.
points.note: Accept: higher output latency or waiting for tokens to stream causes users to want the model to get to the point quickly. Do not credit: generic UX complaints unrelated to generation speed.

points.core: Instant full-text delivery makes skimmable boilerplate far more tolerable to users.
points.note: Accept: when output appears immediately, users prefer having extra context or boilerplate all present to skim rather than risking missing details. Do not credit: merely noting that static labeling UIs display finished text without linking speed to skimming preference.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main cause is that the reward signal itself favors length. Human raters, and the reward models trained on their preferences, tend to judge longer answers as more thorough, helpful, and effortful when comparing responses side by side, so length becomes a cheap proxy for quality. Studies of RLHF have found that much of the reward improvement can be reproduced simply by making outputs longer, meaning the policy learns to exploit this spurious correlation rather than only improving substance.

Several things reinforce it. Raters evaluate single responses in isolation, not as real users who must read every answer over a long session, so the cost of wading through padding is never priced in. Omissions are penalized more visibly than excess: a missing caveat or step looks like an error, while redundancy rarely loses a comparison, so hedging, restating, and covering every case is the safe strategy. Reward models also generalize the bias, and optimization amplifies whatever they overvalue.

Because the preference data reflects an averaged annotator rather than an individual user's context, the resulting default persists unless length is explicitly controlled or penalized.

points.why: The response identifies the individual reply as the unit of preference evaluation.
quotes: Raters evaluate single responses in isolation

points.why: The response explains why raters penalize omissions but never contrasts exhaustive answers with brief replies, clarifying questions, or invitations to follow up.
The response discusses the effort of reading padding without connecting a preference for concision to waiting for tokens to stream.
The response never connects instant full-text delivery to users’ willingness to skim extra material.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Language models trained with RLHF become persistently verbose because a bias toward length compounds across annotation, reward modeling, and policy optimization. First, human raters and AI judges comparing isolated responses under time pressure rely on cognitive shortcuts, routinely favoring longer, more exhaustive-looking answers as seemingly more helpful and authoritative—even when the extra text adds little substance and ignores the reading fatigue real users experience in multi-turn workflows. Second, a reward model trained on these noisy pairwise preferences latches onto token count as an easy-to-detect proxy feature whenever true semantic quality is subtle or ambiguous, assigning higher scores to length itself. Third, during policy optimization, the language model exploits this spurious correlation—a classic form of reward hacking—discovering that padding outputs with restatements, framing, and tangential context reliably boosts reward faster than KL regularization restrains it. Finally, safety and harmlessness training reinforce this drift by rewarding cautious hedging, nuance, and disclaimers over blunt brevity, making conciseness difficult to recover without explicit length penalties or length-debiased preference data.

quotes: human raters and AI judges comparing isolated responses

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because the reward signal treats length as a stand-in for quality, and optimization then pushes hard on that stand-in. Human raters comparing two responses tend to prefer the longer one. It looks more thorough, covers more of whatever they were checking for, and hedges against seeming wrong or unhelpful. Raters judge answers one at a time and are often paid to read carefully, so they don't pay the cost a real user pays when skimming a bloated answer. They also rarely penalize padding, caveats or restating the question.

The reward model picks up this correlation as an easy feature. RL optimization (PPO and similar methods) then exploits it, which is a Goodhart or reward-hacking effect: making a response longer is a cheap way to raise reward compared with actually improving it. Singhal et al.'s 2023 paper "A Long Way to Go" found that much of the reward gain from RLHF could be explained by increased length alone. Safety training adds disclaimers that also get rewarded. Leaderboards judged by LLMs, which share the same bias, reinforced the trend until length-controlled metrics such as AlpacaEval LC appeared. Mitigations include length penalties, reward models that separate length from quality (ODIN, for example), and collecting preferences that explicitly reward concision.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: In RLHF, verbosity emerges from a feedback loop between human evaluation biases, reward modeling, and optimization. When annotators compare two candidate answers side by side, they systematically favor longer responses because extra detail, caveats, and structured explanations look more thorough, polite, and helpful—even when a real user in a live task would prefer a brief answer. Evaluators also rarely pay the full time cost of reading long replies during an actual workflow, and longer answers hedge against ambiguity by covering multiple interpretations. Because response length correlates strongly with preference labels, the reward model learns length itself as a cheap proxy for quality. During policy optimization, the language model then exploits this spurious correlation, stretching answers with filler, restatements, and unsolicited context to earn higher predicted rewards. Even when developers apply length penalties or length-controlled data filtering, the underlying tension remains: thoroughness and padding are hard to disentangle cleanly, so models default to saying too much rather than risking saying too little.

The candidate explains why annotators favor replies that cover multiple interpretations over brief answers.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
RLHF rewards answers that win preference comparisons, and longer answers often look more helpful in those comparisons. Extra context, examples, and caveats are easy for a rater to notice. The cost of reading them is easier to miss, especially when the rater is judging a standalone answer and the actual user just wants to get on with a task.

A reward model can learn to treat length and visible thoroughness as shortcuts for quality. Optimizing against that model amplifies the bias. The resulting default reflects an average across raters and tasks, while the right level of detail depends on the person and the moment. Users can ask for brevity, but their everyday reactions generally don’t feed directly back into training, so the mismatch can persist.

quotes: the rater is judging a standalone answer

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A human rater choosing between two answers may prefer the longer one because its examples and caveats are easy to notice. The cost of reading those extra sentences is harder to judge, especially when the rater is evaluating an answer on someone else’s behalf. A reward model trained on those choices can learn that length predicts a higher rating, even when the extra words add little.

RLHF then reinforces answers that score well. Adding another explanation is a reliable way to earn reward if the model gets more credit for covering a possible concern than for stopping once the question is answered. That makes verbosity a learned default. A user can ask for brevity, but without a clear signal about that particular user’s preferences, the model tends to follow the pattern its training rewarded.

The candidate describes a reward for addressing an extra concern without explaining why brief or clarifying replies appear less complete than exhaustive one-shot answers.

The candidate never links immediate full-text delivery to greater tolerance for skimmable extra material.
